When you're sparring with a steel feder there's a lot more finesse in the bind. Your bind is tighter with the other blade because the steel will notch when the swords cross. they're a little bit sticky almost. It gives you a very good sense for how your opponent is pressuring your sword. I'm definitely for full-contact (assuming a reenforced fending helmet, gloves gambeson, gorget, etc.) You will get hurt, but not badly, just bruises mostly.

Because blousefechten (like in swordfish) is so finesse focused, you'll only rarely hit some one as hard as you want. You'll often commit less because a fully committed strike is easy to redirect. My bread-and-butter is counter-fencing my opponent. Although I'm a little out of practice since I've only been able to properly spar biweekly. But yeah, when it comes to blousefechten there's a very significant degree of finesse required in the blade because receiving a good hit at all is basically you losing the fight. And you're right. Harness is very different from blouse. Harness is much more like wrestling, while blouse is much more distance and blade management.

In most tournaments I've been in (blousefechten tournaments) pommel strikes are completely allowed, and will net you a match-win if you can land it. However, because positioning and distance are so important in blousefechten it's quite difficult to close on a skilled opponent without getting skewered. So managing their blade to close is something you'll have to learn when you start. Most blouse tournaments use steel feders both to be more historical, and because it gives you much more control in the bind. Synthetics don't really 'bind' so much as 'bounce' steel will bind properly and it results in a very different experience.

My issues with it are:

1. Most modern sword makers are doing so with a heavy emphasis on powered grinders to shape the blade after initial forming. That's great if you've gotten it to roughly the right shape, but not if you are cutting it 9ut of a leaf spring. You could run a gun milling shop for a month with the power it would take to grind down one leaf spring to shape.

2. Almost no one making swords now has the experience to forge a sword to the point that it just needs some edge grinding and polishing. If they have that experience already, they are not going to be using leaf springs.

3. Grinding or forging, you need to know enough about heat treating and tempering to actually make it usable. If you don't, you might as well be using wrought iron.
